utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Rodic. May I remind you of the affirmation you took at the beginning which continues to apply. Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, during your examination yesterday, you described, among other things, the damage inflicted upon the Old Town which you were able to see. Can you tell me, of course if you know, what particular buildings in the Old Town were on fire and where are these buildings located?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already drawn this information on this map. This is the house in the Miha Pracata Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know the number?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number. Perhaps it was number 3, 4, or 5. It was the palace in the street of Kuca, Od Kuca across from the Orthodox church, and the house in Siroka Street, and the palace where the Dubrovnik summer festival is held. That is in the Stradun.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: These are then four buildings that you saw burning?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, which I saw when I went out into the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So all these four structures burnt down?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the -- was the Orthodox church damaged?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps. I believe that the glass panes were shattered from the shrapnel and perhaps a few pockmarks on the facade from the shrapnel. There was some damage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know what buildings in Miha Pracata Street, for instance, sustained damage to their facades?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The facade was damaged of this building which had housed number 11, across the street from --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What is the number of the house across the street, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this was 11, then the other one must have been either 8 or 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What kind of damage did it sustain? Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean these two houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this house in Miha Pracata Street 11, which had a stone facade, sustained much damage to the stone. The stone mullions around the door, the entire door, the window, and on the upper storey where there were Venetian binds or, rather, shutters, these were damaged as well, and some other things. On the other side there was also damage, but the facade is made of concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. When you say concrete facade, is this the house that you say is across the street from number 11 in Miha Pracata Street?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The concrete facade showed visible signs of damage, i.e., holes created by shrapnel as well as damage to the windows and doors and the glass panes, et cetera. And in these other streets down -- farther down, there was a lot of debris in the streets and material that had fallen from the damaged roofs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you see -- you probably saw parts of tiles from the roofs when you say debris in the streets.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you see what particular buildings had sustained damage? Can you describe that with precision?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot. I told you which ones were on fire. And as for the damage, I cannot say because material was falling from above, from the roofs. So I cannot say exactly which house was hit. But according to the model, scale model which I saw later, I could see that there were very few roofs that hadn't been damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As regards damage to these two buildings in Miha Pracata Street which you mentioned awhile ago and listed, was this damage -- did this damage -- was it caused by these direct hits that you had described earlier?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this house in Miha Pracata 11, it sustained a direct hit in its roof and others were damaged by shells that had landed in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And when you went about these streets in the Old Town as you were leaving --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: -- do you know which one was directly hit and was damaged by direct impact?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A street or a house?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Buildings. A building.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably these that were on fire had been directly hit. And of course these houses nearby there were bricks -- there were bricks and roof tiles and debris, meaning that they had sustained hits in their roofs. There was fragments of shrapnel in the Stradun, and there were -- shells had landed on Onofrius fountain and directly on the Stradun street. One could see that facades on both sides of the street, the Stradun that is, were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you say concretely what buildings you saw with damaged facades there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one in Siroka Street towards the exit at the Ploce Gate -- no, the Pile Gate. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What buildings? Can you describe to us what buildings these were? The last one when you leave Siroka Street, the first one to the left, the first one to the right? Can you give us a more specific description if you do not know the exact number?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first house to the -- on the street next to the festival palace, which is across the street and has a bookstore in the basement next to which is the Croatian lottery building, and then the -- further on towards the Pile Gate, the Franciscan Monastery, and the Friars' Minor Church. And then the tourist association building and further down the Onofrius fountain. Towards the Pile Gate, also the gate itself is damaged, and so --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you say exactly what was damaged on all these buildings that you could see? Building by building, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- well, on these buildings which are on the Stradun, the facades were lifted, the stone mullions around the doors, the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we go building by building so you can describe building by building for me.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: For instance, in Siroka Street, did you pass through it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What buildings did you see were damaged?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said this house which was ablaze, the house next to it in which there is a goldsmith, the door was damaged. The facade, the stone facade as well. Then there was shrapnel-inflicted damage. There were pockmarks in the stone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you say more specifically what specific part of the facade, what part of the building?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Predominantly the lower part of the building, the -- where there were more shrapnel marks, where the stone mullions of the facades were damaged. And the damage was more or less the same on all these buildings because all these were stone buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say -- when you say stone mullions, can you describe for me what particular element of the house this is.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These stone mullions are elements of stone which are around the door in a single piece as a lintel. And they are called actually in our language stone needles, stone mullions. This is what I call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You mean the entrance door?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the entrance doors, the windows, those which have ornamental stone elements and are decorated with them. Depends on the house in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you say that generally speaking this was -- this was damaged on all houses.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the best of my recollection, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Meaning on all these houses in the streets that you walked through until you left the Old Town. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is the streets Od Puca, Siroka, and the Stradun.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you notice there was any house that had not sustained damage?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were few houses that didn't have at least some pockmarks on the stone facades effected by fragments of shrapnel. There were few that hadn't sustained damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you said that you hadn't even noticed that you were hurt until Mato Skocko told you that you were hurt.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also said that in this store of yours, you cleaned the superficial wounds, and sometime around 11.30 had left the building. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: A day later, you had routine treatment administered to you in the infirmary in Gruz.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that you were perhaps scratched by stone shards?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible I could have been, but probably because of the width of the hole and the depth of the cutting, it was more probably inflicted by a piece of shrapnel. But it may have been stone, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Have you talked to the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And in any other place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter believes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you give them a written statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just this one in Dubrovnik when they were there in October and September.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was a statement compiled in writing about this interview and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this on the 24th of September, 2003?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I cannot recall the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Had anyone gotten in touch with you prior to that date?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the gentleman from the Tribunal did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps some 15 or 20 days or a month before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Had you made an appointment for that particular meeting or what?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had an agreement in principle to the effect that they would not be coming to Dubrovnik but that I should come here to The Hague to testify, and in view of the fact that I was getting ready to travel to Australia, I wouldn't. And then later they agreed that they would come to Dubrovnik for our interview, and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And this first interview was in August 2003 or, rather, July and August?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. About that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And prior to the year 2003, no one had gotten in touch with you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know how exactly they got in touch with you, how was it specifically you that they found?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It's been 12 years since then, and no one spoke to you until last year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a bit taken by surprise too. Probably -- I don't know. I don't know. Perhaps it was because of Mr. Skocko's statement or somebody else's statement. Maybe. I'm just guessing, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mato Skocko tell you about making a statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, because we haven't worked together since 1995 -- or was it 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said that as far as Tonci Skocko is concerned, you carried him into the car.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a more specific description in terms of the actual place involved?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's towards the end of the street of Miha Pracata where Mr. Skocko came in his car.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this towards the music school?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is way down by the intersection between Miha Pracata and the street Od Puca.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say "down there," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean at the intersection of the street Od Puca and Miha Pracata.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How far away is that from your shop?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a hundred metres. About a hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you and Mato Skocko carry Tonci these 100 metres?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was I, Mato, Mr. Skerlj, and another gentleman whose name I don't know. He happened to be there. He was a customer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As you were carrying him, you noticed where the injury was. Please don't hurry with your answer.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not while we were carrying him but as we were placing him into the car. We wanted him to lie down on the back seat, so as I was pulling him by the shoulders, by the arms, that's how his T-shirt moved, and I could see the injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why didn't you mention this in your statement from the month of September? You didn't mention that you carried Tonci Skocko to the car, and you did not mention that you saw where he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did state that, but perhaps they did not record all of it. Because we talked for four hours, and it's about a two-page record only.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your statement there's not a single word about this.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. You have to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your statement, it says that you could not see where he was wounded. "We could not see at all where he had been wounded." That's the sentence here in your statement.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said. In the shop we couldn't see because there wasn't any blood. There wasn't anything. And we were trying to resuscitate a man who was already dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was it only here that they showed you where Tonci Skocko was wounded?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you see a picture?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your statement, it also says that it was only later, after Tonci was taken to hospital, you found out that he was hit by shrapnel in the heart. That's what you said to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I put it that way. Perhaps -- well, I said that I found out only when Mr. Skocko came back from the hospital, I found out that Tonci was dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This is what you say: "Mato then rushed him to the hospital. At the hospital, it was diagnosed that shrapnel had pierced his heart."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what they diagnosed at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Again, you learned about all of that subsequently; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did I learn?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, where the shrapnel had hit him.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw the hole, and then when Mato Skocko returned from the hospital, he said that this, what we call shrapnel, hit him directly in the heart and that, therefore, he could not be saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And that is what Mato Skocko said to you when he got back from hospital, when he came back to the shop?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: However, Mato Skocko, in his statement, says: "A friend of mine and I put Tonci in the car and set out to the hospital straight away." He does not mention you at all, that he -- when he was carrying Tonci to the car that he was helped by you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to ask him about that if that's what he stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where does the wife of Mato Skocko work or, rather, where did she work then?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I've forgotten. I don't know whether she worked anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Have you heard perhaps that she worked at the Argentina Hotel?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me why Mato Skocko returned to the shop from hospital, why?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. He took the car up there, left it there because the car didn't really have any tyres, or, rather, the tyres were punctured. So then he returned to the shop where the rest of us had been, those who had stayed behind, and he probably could not go home anyway. And he had no one to go with because he was alone at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How long did he stay at the shop? I mean, you say that you stayed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. until 11.30. Did he stay after you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about such details. I think we all left more or less at the same time. Perhaps a bit earlier, I don't know. Because I think that Mr. Skerlj also went with him, because his wife hadn't known that the son was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, don't you find that strange; if he finds out in hospital that his son got killed, he comes back to the shop and he sits there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mato Skocko says in his statement: "In hospital, the physician confirmed to me that my son was dead and that he had been dead for a while. The doctor gave me a tranquiliser, a shot. I was in a state of shock. Soon after that, I fled from the hospital to see my wife at the hotel to tell her that our son was dead."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects to my learned colleague -- our learned colleague Mr. Rodic reading extracts from a statement of a witness who has not given evidence and the evidence isn't before the Tribunal and asking the -- this witness here to comment on it. He shouldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the position, Mr. Rodic. If you want to raise the matter, you can go so far as to say, "Isn't it the position that the gentleman left the hospital and went to the hotel to see his wife?" The witness will either agree with you or disagree with you. You can't then go on to say, "Well, this is what he said in his statement." I think you'll be familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. Yes, I shall rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, after being in the hospital, didn't Mato go directly to see his wife to tell her about their son's death?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what happened. As for his own statement, ask Mr. Skocko about it. I know what I know. I know what happened, and what he stated, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So it is your assertion that he was with you at the shop until 11.30 and that together, on the 6th of December, you set out from the shop via Stradun to your homes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that Mr. Skocko came to the shop from the hospital. Now, I don't know exactly whether we went together after that, whether it was half an hour sooner or later, but we left the shop more or less around the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: A few minutes ago you said you left the shop together.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I can't remember. Perhaps he left a bit earlier, perhaps we left together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you have any medical documents related to the scratches on your chin and leg?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some from the regional doctor, but now I don't know where it is. I didn't need it. Perhaps it's been mislaid somewhere. Perhaps it's still in the house. I don't know. I never needed it for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you have a military ID, military booklet?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your military booklet, do you have the duration of your participation in the war; to, from?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know which period was entered exactly?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was from the 23rd. From the 23rd -- no. Around the 20th of February 2002 and until mid 2003. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That is last year and the year before last.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I misspoke. It was 1992. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And are there any entries from 1991 in your military service booklet?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have the booklet here with you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have it in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you provide a copy to the Court, to the Trial Chamber, of your military service booklet with this information?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Finally, can I ask you the following question: You said that you carried food in mess tins.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're carried on the back, too, and I don't exactly know what the word for such tins is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But you did see such mess tins when you were in the army, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, like that or something similar. All of it's the same basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you know how many food rations you were supposed to carry?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who gave you the exact number of rations that were supposed to be carried to Srdj?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't carry any rations. We carried three or four of these mess tins and two or three sacks of bread, and that was all we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But who gave you this exact amount that you then carried?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The van that brought this in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this a military van?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a civilian van, but it was driven by a military man.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the soldiers who were at Srdj? Were they given information that you were coming in, that you shouldn't be shot at?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't it have been risky for you to go there, especially on foot, without having the soldiers at Srdj informed about who was coming?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably, but I don't know whether they were informed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were -- were any of you who went up there armed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What did -- what did he have?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An ordinary rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was he uniformed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had boots and the military JNA jacket. A shirt and a jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was he there to secure you or to escort you up there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he went in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did he also return with you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay up there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We just left the things there and returned. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me where exactly you deposited your load?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the entrance to the Srdj fort from the lower side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers up there at Srdj?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't, because we didn't go in. We didn't go inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers there at all?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that. Probably there were when we were carrying food up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have finished my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Re, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is. Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, Mr. Rodic asked you about where Mr. Tonci Skocko lived, and you said it was in Zlatni Potok. Where is Zlatni Potok? Is it in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlatni Potok is to the east or south-east of the Old Town towards the Hotel Belvedere, from the Ploce Gate [as interpreted] towards the Hotel Belvedere.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How far is it from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Rodic asked you about an assignment you had in the Territorial Defence. This is at page 35 of yesterday's transcript. The question was: "And what particular assignment did you have in the Territorial Defence?" To which your answer was: "It was the same thing as the training I had received in the army, which is the -- an operator of Maljutkas." Question: "In the period from 1983 to 1991, did you participate in any military exercises as a reservist?" Answer: "No, I did not," and so on. Your evidence the day before, or your evidence earlier was of doing your JNA military training in Kosovo in 1982 and 1983 and specifically on Maljutkas artillery. What level of or what type of skills are required for a person to operate a Maljutka missile?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we and the then-JNA, some were members of crews and some had been trained to become operators to be able to guide a missile to its target. It was a guided missile. So that this training took some five or six months. We used simulators for the training.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How specialised was the training to operate Maljutka wire-guided missiles?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite get the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question is about the specialisation required to operate a Maljutka wire-guided missile. How -- what level of specialisation is required to learn to operate one as opposed to other missiles?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I was trained to operate the Maljutka. What the specialisation level was, this is something that the military authorities had determined themselves, namely whether a person was capable of being thus trained or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know how the training to operate Maljutkas differed from training to operate other types of missiles you may have encountered in your JNA training? When I say "missiles," I also mean projectiles, shells, mortars of the like.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Maljutka was a missile, an anti-tank -- an anti-armour, rather, missile which was a guided one which was manually guided towards its target so that we had to be trained in this guidance of that missile using the simulators provided to us by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how did that differ from the training to operate other types of mortars or missiles or shells?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a completely different type of training, because mortars probably also involve practical drills, practical exercises. I don't really know. But we exclusively used these electric simulators for training.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you ever use live ammunition in your training in the JNA or in your several exercises as a reservist?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, while I was serving the JNA, we only had one exercise where this live ammunition where all the 50 of us who had completed this training, all the -- of the 50 of us who had completed this training, only two had actually fired the rocket. But later when I was in the Territorial Defence, I never even saw this missile. We only used these simulators in the military facilities or the barracks in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what did you learn in your training about the cost of Maljutkas relative to that of other projectiles used by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know the actual cost, but they did say that the Maljutkas were much more expensive than these other projectiles. That is what they said to us then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday in cross-examination, you were describing to Mr. Rodic a flag with an emblem that had been displayed on certain buildings, and your answer was: "It went like this and it went like that and it says Monument of Culture in the middle." At that point you were drawing with your hands something on the table in front of you. I'm going to ask you to draw a picture of what you saw on the banners hanging from buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be given a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a white flag inside -- banner. Inside was this arrow, and on it was written "Monument of Culture."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember what colour the writing and the arrow was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was either blue or black. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just put the date on the bottom and please sign your name on the bottom of that piece of paper. It's the 24th of February, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we, Your Honour, see the drawing on the ELMO before that, because we didn't have an occasion to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Jovic, Mr. Rodic asked you this morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm waiting an exhibit number. I think I might have jumped in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was too slow, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P76.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic asked you this morning whether you had any medical records relating to the injuries you received on the 6th of December, 1991. You said you couldn't find them at home. Have you made any attempts to obtain those records from the clinic where you were treated in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days before my departure for The Hague, when a lady from the Tribunal called me and asked me whether I had any documentation - this could have been some two days before my trip - I looked for it so -- and I couldn't find anything at home. I went to the health centre, they couldn't find anything either. And I can try when I go back, when I get back, and to find it and fax it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jovic, for your time that you've spent here and your assistance, and I am pleased to be able to tell you are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re, was there left from Friday night the question of tendering some exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Somers can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're going to give up the job, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Giving it up to the boss. Thank you, Your Honour. In fact there was raised the photographs from the autopsy, and Mr. Rodic very generously said he was no longer going to object and we were just going to handle the process at the beginning of this week's sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it convenient to do it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. I thank Ms. Somers for reminding me of that. It certainly is convenient. I formally offer into evidence the photographs, the two photographs of the autopsies, the bodies of Mr. Tonci Skocko and Mr. Pavo Urban. And also MFI 70, which is the autopsy report of the 7th of December, 1991, in respect of which Dr. Ciganovic testified. Those are the three exhibits I offer into evidence. MFI --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did the photograph of Mr. Urban become Exhibit P71?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the two photographs were marked for identification respectively P71 and P72, and the report was marked for identification MFI P70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, in view of the position that was indicated on Friday evening, those three documents which are presently marked for identification will become exhibits with the same number. Is that all of those?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That is the three, yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I did indicate on Friday evening that it would be convenient to deal with the legal argument at the end of this witness, but this witness took quite a bit longer than anticipated. I'm conscious of the delays with witnesses. Would it be more convenient to hear the next witness before going back to that legal argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Indeed it would, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a problem for you, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it isn't, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we might follow that course then, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I would ask Ms. Usher to usher in Mr. Djelo Jusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I wonder whether you would be kind enough to take that card in your hand and read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish all of you a good morning, and I will be more than pleased to read this out. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. If you could state your name, please, your full name, for the record. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: I am Djelo Jusic, born in Dubrovnik in 1939.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And your present address, please.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Lazarina number 3, Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And perhaps you could tell us your religion.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, your current occupation, as even Mr. Rodic knows, because I know he's waiting for your evidence, is composer and conductor. Could you enlighten us to a few details about your career, what you're presently doing --

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So your present position?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Officially I'm the conductor of the Dubrovnik Symphony Orchestra. I write music all the time, either for children or for the Symphony Orchestra. I write oratoria, pop music, musicals, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Is your musical activity confined to Dubrovnik? Do you have a more international appeal?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: My music, well, I published more than 5.000 minutes of my music. My music is performed in New York, Vienna, Belgrade. In Montenegro I hear it over the radio, that they play my music. In Croatia, then London, Paris, Moscow, Milan, Rome, Dubrovnik, Zagreb. Before the war, I was a very popular musician, especially with my orchestra, The Troubadours of Dubrovnik, and particularly in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to Belgrade in a minute, sir, but I believe you've had the honour of having your music played in the Vatican; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992 during the worst attack against Dubrovnik -- well, actually, I should say that I have this small children's choir in Dubrovnik called The Small Singing Dubrovnik, and I was invited in 1992 to Vatican, we were received by the Holy Father, and we performed my music. I conducted the choir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Has your music ever been played in Belgrade, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Countless number of times. I was very popular in Belgrade. I even won a few prizes at festivals in Belgrade. And with my orchestra, The Troubadours of Dubrovnik, I toured Serbia and Montenegro countless number of times. Our popularity was truly great. I recorded a few LPs in Belgrade. I had solo concerts at the big trade union hall in Belgrade. I actually published five LP records with the Belgrade company RTB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, in 1991, the start of 1991, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Until 1990 I lived in Zagreb for about 15 years because Zagreb is a big cultural centre where there are studios, where there are concert halls, and that's what I missed in Dubrovnik. But I also did my recordings in Skopje, Macedonia, then in Belgrade, then in Zagreb, Ljubljana, and many European cities at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, at a certain stage, sir, you left Zagreb. Where did you go when you left Zagreb, and when was that?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: When I felt that there was political turbulence in my former country, I felt that there was danger looming over my hometown of Dubrovnik, so I went back. My music is related to Dubrovnik. I simply had to be there. I had to defend the town. I had many friends throughout our former country, and I believed that they would not touch Dubrovnik. Perhaps I was a bit conceited. I said at least because of me they would not do anything bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So that's what you meant by defence, is it, artistic defence?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, because muses should never fall silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, when did you actually arrive in Dubrovnik in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: In the spring. In the spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And the address where you set up home?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Lazarina number 3, as you told you awhile ago. That's where I have my own apartment, and I moved into that apartment in 1973.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Mr. Usher to place a map on the ELMO for you. And I would request that you point out where your house is in relation to the Old Town. This will have significance as we proceed and hear your evidence. I have small maps of the map. Ms. Usher, if you could hand this out.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: This is the Old Town of Dubrovnik -- may I speak now? May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If we could move the map slightly up so we could see the Old Town, and maybe reduce the picture. Zoom out, as it were.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: This is the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: This is the Excelsior Hotel. Above the Hotel Excelsior is my apartment, and there is a panorama of the island of Lokrum and the entire town from my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, please take a blue pen - which is positioned to the side - mark with the letter A the approximate position of your house.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, mark with the letter B Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could put that aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Might I request that to be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P77.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about moving to Dubrovnik. Did any other people move to Dubrovnik apart from yourself, any other particular category of persons?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. Actually, people were surprised why I had come to Dubrovnik, because many people were leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: To the Old Town of Dubrovnik did people move?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: People were not moving in. They were fleeing in panic when the attacks against Croatia started from the direction of Konavle, to be precise, and also Molunat, Cavtat. They were fleeing. They were seeking shelter in the hotels of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Did they seek shelter in any other places, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: They sought shelter in the Dubrovnik fortresses; for example, St. Ivan, Revelin, Minceta, the Rupe museum. Some were even staying at monasteries and churches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that people sought shelter in the Old Town essentially, as well as the hotels that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Not only in the Old Town. There's a peninsula called Babin Kuk on the western side, then there is the Hotel Palace, President, Argos, Minceta. Those are the hotels at Babin Kuk. That's where people sought shelter as well as at the Libertas Hotel, the Lero Hotel, the Petka Hotel. That would be about it. Those were the hotels where people sought shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Do you have an approximate estimate, sir, for the number of people who were seeking shelter in the Old Town -- in the shelters in the Old Town that you mentioned? If you don't, say, "I don't."

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that definitely the entire population of Konavle left and sought shelter there. They left their homes and they moved within the Old City walls or those hotels that were outside the Old City.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Let us move on to the month of October. Now, from your balcony and from your forays into the Old Town, what happened to the Old Town in the month of October?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, one morning around 5.00 -- we in Dubrovnik - I have to say this - are very fearful of earthquakes because this an earthquake-prone area. However, what we heard then was something new, something different, a different sound. So people were fleeing from their houses panic-stricken. And then we realised that some shells were falling. They were coming from the north-east. Not of the east but the north-east, from the behind the hills near my home, near the Old City. And that's when these boats, I think they are called gunboats, opened fire too. They were there near Dubrovnik. These were warships, and they had been there for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And that, as you say, is at the beginning of the month of October. You were awoken early in the morning -- yes, sir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in mid-October. I cannot give you the exact date, but around that time. People were panic-stricken, fleeing to shelters, and everybody thought it would be only that one morning or perhaps a day or two, but it went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to the Old Town in the month of October. Are you aware of anything happening to the Old Town in the month of October as a result of this shelling that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: In the Old Town, the inhabitants of Dubrovnik thought that since Dubrovnik was an old town and it was part of UNESCO Heritage, and people, sensible people, of course, thought that nothing would fall on the Old Town and there would be no shooting there. However, one day a shell fell into Boskoviceva Street and it broke a very old balcony because it hit straight into the house. I think it was on that day or the next day that 15 ambassadors came. They came by boat from Cavtat. They probably flew into Cavtat. They came to see whether it was possible at all that somebody actually had fired at the Old Town of Dubrovnik that was part of UNESCO Heritage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, how did you know about this visiting party of ambassadors?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, some of us who were careless enough left our homes, and we strolled about town. They were escorted by the JNA, the Yugoslav army. Then Mr. Hrvoje Kacic, a diplomat from Dubrovnik, was there and he told me who these people were. Then also I recognised some of them. The Italian had a very typical cap with that little feather on it. There were about ten or so other citizens who were watching this, and they couldn't believe their own eyes. We thought that this was a stray bullet or a stray shell, whatever it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Before we leave the month of October, I'd like to ask you about the status of the Dubrovnik infrastructure in that month. Electricity and water; what can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: For centuries, Dubrovnik has had this water supply. So water and electricity were never a problem in Dubrovnik. However, either during this first attack or during a following attack, it was the power plant that supplies Dubrovnik with electricity was destroyed, and of course there was no electricity, naturally, and then there was no water either. When there was no water, people were in panic, and they started buying food supplies. So Dubrovnik was emptied. It was an unhappy town, feeling shame and disgrace, and people really started thinking about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the minutes before the morning interval -- we're going to show a video that you filmed, but in the minutes before the interval, perhaps we could clarify how it came about that you videotaped the goings-on in the town of Dubrovnik in the month of November and December. You have a video camera, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but before that I would like to mention a particular piece of information that I find interesting and most regrettable. The first shell that was fired from this gunboat hit a house in my neighbourhood 50 metres away from my house, and this is where a great poet of Dubrovnik got killed, a personal friend of mine, an ethnic Serb. His name is Milan Milisic. He was very well liked and he was a popular writer. I think that at the time he was employed at the Marin Drzic Theatre in Dubrovnik. I have a Panasonic MD7 camera. I think that's the make. I got it in the 1980s because I have three children and six grandchildren, so I needed it, and also the most beautiful ships in the world come to the harbour of Dubrovnik, so I enjoyed taking pictures of that too. So it was my hobby. I started doing this for a very naive reason. Actually in 1991, in the summer, the Yutel team came to Dubrovnik, although their headquarters by then were in Sarajevo. So they wanted to record a film about me and my life and work. However, in October or November, they called me from Sarajevo, and they asked me the following: "We know where you live. Can you tell us the truth? Because Belgrade says that you are setting fire to tyres in Dubrovnik in order to pretend that you're being attacked, whereas Zagreb says that you actually are under attack." I spoke as a reporter on the news programme of Yutel then, but then all of a sudden I thought of actually recording this from my balcony because you can see the entire Panorama of Dubrovnik there, that is to say the sea and the island and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you, as we will later see, videotaped some of the events in November and December.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: It was very important for me that I recorded these first moments and also later on. I wanted the world to know about this. In the Libertas Hotel in Dubrovnik, there was an office of Zagreb television, Croatian television. So I gave these recordings to them, and then this footage was sent further on into the world, CNN, Sky News, and other major TV stations telecast this. So this was the first recording of what was actually happening in Dubrovnik that was shown throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember exactly what there is on the film, the video film that we will be showing to the Court in due course?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: For example, there is one particular clip that received many compliments throughout the world. Since they had already started shooting, we thought that they would not touch the Old Town itself out of respect for it. So then people, for example, brought their cars to the Old City of Dubrovnik. And a man drove his new car, a Mazda, I think it was, into the Old City port. So then I had this really interesting footage. All of a sudden we started learning all these new words, Maljutka, shells, words that we didn't use in our lives before that. And then this Maljutka hit the car, and then the car flew into the air. If that is the footage that you're going to play, that's what we're going to see. It's one of the first things recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, perhaps, Your Honours, this might be a convenient point to break, because we will see the video in due course, and what I will ask the witness to do is to give us a running commentary of the film as it progresses. He will stop the film when he feels there is a need to expand upon what is seen in the film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In that case, then, Mr. Kaufman, I think we will have our morning break now and then return for the viewing of the film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, a few more clarificatory questions before we get into the video. Did you film this footage that we're about to see or did anyone else help you?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Everything that we're going to view on this topic I did myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And you handed this video that we're about to see to the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you mentioned doing some filming in the month of November. Let's start the film and see what happened in the month of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, that's your balcony, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: This is -- no. The balcony is in the next clip. This is an overview above my flat. Stop for a minute. You can see the number of boats that we have in our city harbour. There are hundreds of them. Over the next ten days, 80 per cent of these boats had burnt on account of the shells, which was a tragedy for the citizens of Dubrovnik, because Dubrovnik citizens are very close to the sea, and I know this because of the way I felt. This here is my -- where my boat was, and when this happened, I said dear God, let anything happen, but do not let my boat sink. Can we go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Before we go on, if you can have a look to where the arrow is pointing. What do we see here?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: I can't see the arrow -- oh, yes, I can. This is where the car was which would get hit in the next minute, and a huge chunk of which would then fly up to this bell tower, the top of the belfry. You will be able to see that. Here we have ships, boats, actually, that were all burnt down in later attacks. These are all tourist and fishing boats, private small boats people use for their own enjoyment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, please continue watching, and I will stop the video in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, we have a transcript prepared of what was exactly said there and we will submit that to the Court in due course. Perhaps you can tell us what you were commenting on there.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, the first voice which you heard is my voice, and the second one is Mr. Luksa, a neighbour of mine, who was a very jovial chap, and he was -- he liked his drink. And he said that the enemy were drunk and that they were perhaps shooting because they were drunk. At the time, it was quite witty, but a bit later we didn't find it that funny at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, before the break, sir, you mentioned the new argot that you had been learning at that time, terms such as Maljutkas. You also are a musician and know a bit about acoustics, so perhaps you can tell us what type of ordnance this was, from your own perspective.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the first time I heard about the term Maljutka, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 150-millimetre shell, or a machine-gun of 80, but we saw some threads, some traces, and they told us that this Maljutka was being guided like a children's toy and that this was done by a screen so that it could target with precision its desired target, and that is when I found out that its name was Maljutka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We're going to move the video on slightly, and this is about a minute into your video film, still in the month of November, as you say. Please watch the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. This is the car that was blown up, which actually flew into the air, rather. And I'm really proud as a little boy for having taken this recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is dramatic. Now, that's the one from November. There are two further days which appear on this video. Can you tell the Court which days those are.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: There was already too much excitement for me to actually jot down the date on the screen. What my objective was to turn the camera on and to indeed record this, and of course to get away from the place as soon as possible, because at the very next minute, you can hear also that there was shooting from some quarter and that the shell actually whizzed right by me or in front of my face towards the Old Town. I was quite calm when I was recording this, but when I looked at these recordings a year ago, I was really scared out of my wits because of how courageous I had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, we will now move to the month of December. We will continue with your video later. Before we do that, let's do things chronologically, and I would like to take you to the 5th of December. The 5th of December, being a musician, was a very special day for you, wasn't it, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, 1991, all the cultural world - I'm talking about the whole planet - was marking the 200th anniversary of Mozart's death. So I and my friends organised a concert and to honour him and of course to perform Mozart's music, and this was held in the Dubrovnik cathedral. This was about 11 a.m. because it couldn't be performed in the evening because of the curfew that had had already been imposed there was no power, to we had to perform at a time of day when one could best read the sheet scores of music. Of course, word came out about this because Radio Dubrovnik had also announced that the Dubrovnik musicians would be marking Mozart's anniversary and as Radio Dubrovnik can also be heard in Montenegro as well as in Trogir, everybody could hear about this date. So that sometime around 7.00 in the morning, right here behind my back you can see the hill of Bosanka and Zarkovica. They brought a loud public address system there, a very loud one, and they played traditional war -- Serbian songs accompanied by the traditional gusle instrument. This echoed, reverberated all around Dubrovnik and the Elafiti islands. The idea was to disrupt our marking of Mozart's anniversary, and perhaps there was another message there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Did it disrupt the performance of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's music?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: It absolutely did disrupt, but people commented that anyway, this is where the difference lay between us, between these peoples, that this was where the line of distinction was so that -- we were Mozart and they were a gusle. Of course, I have nothing against a gusle, let everybody play what they like, but as a musician, I feel that nobody should interfere with other people's business and let us all rejoice in our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Let's move to the 6th of December. What time did you wake up on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: About 5.15, 5.20 in the morning. There was this great fracas. Something started and we thought that the shelling at that time was the heaviest. However, at that time there was a fortissimo from all instruments blaring out, not only at the outskirts of town but also at the very centre, the core of the city, and that was the famous 6th of December when Dubrovnik was devastated, degraded, when hundred year old palaces and churches were demolished, when archives were torn down, archives housing, inter alia, documents of the great Serbian Empire, its Tsar Dusan and the Nemanjic dynasty. At least for those reasons I find it hard to understand why they opened fire at the one-thousand-year-old archives of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You've used the term in the transcript, sir, "the core of the city." By that do you mean the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: When I speak, I can speak about the part which is within the ramparts. That is the Old Town, that was where I went, inside from rampart to rampart. I never went outside so that I have no information about what was going on outside the walls. I can, however, assert that for countless times I was in the Old City in the right place at the right time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You talked about a fortissimo of instruments in the morning. Now, by "instruments" I know you're a musician, sir, but what do you mean by the word "instruments"?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Of course musical designations forte, fortissimo and forte fortissimo with the -- forte fortissimo is too strong and forte forte fortissimo is the strongest, which is actually the very limits that a human ear can consume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And by "instruments" you mean?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Of course this is something which is beautiful in music, but what I mean, I'm saying -- I mean mortars and cannon and the overflying aircraft. That is what I meant by using this term. The only thing which should have happened was for something to come out from the earth, but that didn't happen, fortunately. Now, talking in musical terms, for instance, if a shell in Dubrovnik had between 15 or 20 reverberations so that at the moment of impact you couldn't actually tell if it had fallen in this or that particular spot or place because of these echoing, there was a sort of cacophony, as it is called, and it was mayhem. It's a wonder that not many people went crazy because of the -- everything which was going on and the flying shrapnel and whatchamacallit. There was a lot of to'ing and fro'ing, people running about, seeking shelter, seeking places to hide. We were not exactly sure what was going on but we knew that there was shelling and one could see that there was shelling from the east side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Can you talk about the intensity of the shelling on the 6th of December? Did you --

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: This one single attack started immediately with this fortissimo fortissimo intensity so that, as far as one could tell by hearing, there was shooting from behind and from the Bosanka Zarkovica hills, and there was this terrible sound coming from the direction of Cavtat, from the left side where the Dubrovnik airport is, and then there were also battleships, gunboats that were opening fire, but not -- they didn't remain in a single spot. They kept cruising. They kept moving and opening fire, and you can see that. You will be able to see that on the film, on the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, what I'm talking about is the 6th --

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I have to add, since Dubrovnik is a city under UNESCO protection, in lots of places it had very important palaces and mansions, and houses, libraries flying UNESCO flags, and one had the impression that they were opening fire at precisely those places flying such flags as their desired targets, and it is precisely those buildings that sustained the most damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, in due course we will see those flags. We have a lot to get through, so if we could perhaps ask you to make your answers concise. Now, sir you talked about a fortissimo. Now, was there, in musical terms let me put it, a diminuendo in the shelling at any time on that day, a lessening of intensity?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in music terms, nobody was enjoying this music. People had to flee for dear life. And I myself was also hidden and perhaps I couldn't hear everything properly, but it is a fact that this lasted from 5.15 until about 5.15 in the evening. So there was a continuous process with ups and downs, shall we put it, but I didn't have the concentration to listen to it voluntarily. I was forced to listen to it, but I certainly did not enjoy it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Did you witness the shelling of the Old Town until 5.15 from your house or from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, we're now about to see the part of the footage which is the most important of all, precisely this attack on the 5th [as interpreted]. I recorded until perhaps midday or 1.00, until my battery ran out. But I remember definitely that it lasted until 5.00 or 5.30. And I'm sure that it lasted that much. I would like to concentrate on the movie, because it is self-explanatory. It tells it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, we will get to the movie in a moment, but you said the attack on the 5th. Now, you were conducting Mozart on the 5th. Did the attack take place on the 5th or on another day?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: No. The attack was the -- the main attack was on the 6th of December, but the 5th was Mozart as an overture to this eroica, shall we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, because the transcript read something else. That's why I asked to correct you. Now, if we can actually return to your video. I'm not actually going to show you the 6th. I'm going to take you to the day after. The full video will be presented to Their Honours and they will have a full opportunity to see everything that is contained and everything that happened on the 6th insofar as it was filmed by you, but I would like to take you to the day after, the 7th of December. I would like you to tell us what you did on the 7th of December.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: As the curfew was lifted on the 6th of December which had been on in Dubrovnik for months before that, one couldn't leave, go outside after 9.00 in the evening, so on the 6th it was lifted, and of course it was lifted also on the next day. So in the morning on the 7th, I went towards the city with my camera on, recording what I thought ought to be recorded, was important enough to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So let us indeed turn to the video. Now, this is found at approximately 13 minutes -- 13 minutes 37. I'll get my assistant and colleague Ms. McCreath to find the relevant part on the video.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I don't have it -- oh, yes, I do have it. Please stop now. We are in the Old Town, and we are below the Dominican cloister, and up this wall is the central part of the church, the altar, et cetera. Here there is a shell which is at least one metre long which I could see later after they had pulled it out. It hit the area underneath the church, but it did not explode. It actually was lodged in the stone, and one could only imagine what would have happened had it exploded. So this is on the east side of the Dominican Monastery's church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: At this stage, sir, before we continue, I'm going to ask for a map to be placed in front of you. We will hopefully track your course through the Old Town on this morning, the morning of the 7th of December. If you would kindly indicate with the blue pen that will be provided to you your course on that day. So if perhaps you could put a small letter A by the first point you've indicated, the place to the side of the Dominican Monastery where you discovered that shell.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: On this side, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did you write a little A there, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Near the church, you mean. Where I started, where I set out?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And put a little A by the place you found the unexploded ordnance, as you say. A tiny little A.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let us continue. Once again if you could look at your monitor now, and when you feel that there's a need to stop to expand upon what we're seeing here, please indicate by saying "Stop." I might find the need to also stop the video and ask you a few questions. Please try and indicate, sir, as many buildings as possible for the benefit of the Court as you go through. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we are entering the Old Town, as you can see. You can see the stones and the tiles that have fallen off the roofs. Please stop at this point. Here already after the first attacks the people of Dubrovnik boarded up their monuments in order to protect them, but of course this was really no protection to speak of for the -- against those shells. This was the portico of a church built several hundred years ago. This is exactly where the shell hit it. You can see the impact mark, the hole, and we are now restoring this main portico to the Dominican church. Thank you. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One citizen telling me to go into another street to see the devastation there. Here we have some stone because this is where a sculptor has his artistic studio. On the ground you can see rubble. Stop now, please. This building here, this is the library or, rather, the Dubrovnik archives, several hundred years old, keeping documents on all the countries of the former Balkans. And I failed to comprehend why they opened fire at it. The roof also caved in -- rather, fell down, and there are also visible traces of shell impact on it. We can go on, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, before we do, could you perhaps provide an exact address for that building, the archive?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: I'll show it to you now. Here it is. Here is the wall. Here is the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, on your map, with the blue pen that will be provided to you, if you could mark the letter B by the Dubrovnik archive. We will follow your path through the Old Town. A tiny little letter B, please.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: My learned colleague Mr. Re suggests that we might use a finer pen than that. I thank him for that. Let us continue, sir. Please look at the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you stop for a moment here, please. Later on, when we get into the main street, you will see -- or, rather, you saw here that there is this yellow colour, this yellow marking on the wall. Later on, we're going to see on a house that there is something yellow like that too. And I asked an observer -- fine. Fine. I remember that that's where the yellow appeared. So let's go on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, as we go through, perhaps you could say where we are.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: Now we are entering the main street of Dubrovnik, the most famous street in Dubrovnik, called Stradun. This is the port. Now we're entering the main street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, we will do that, but I see a pipe. If you could follow the arrow. What is this?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: This is a pipe, because the previous evening when Dubrovnik was on fire, it was quite literally on fire because there was this strong wind that was fanning the flames, there was a curfew because there was an international SOS that had been declared. So our Minister Rudolf received a promise from the side from where the shooting was coming from that there would be a lull in the shooting for a while. Indeed on the 7th there was no shooting in order to extinguish the fire in Dubrovnik. The firemen brought these pipes. We had no water whatsoever. So this pipe leads to the harbour and seawater was brought through those pipes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see the Franciscan cloister here. That was also hit. Then the festival building of Dubrovnik. You can see the Church of St. Blaise that was hit here. Here is the UNESCO sign. Could you just raise this up a bit so that you can see what is here on the facade? Hundreds of years old. This is the Church of St. Blaise, St. Blaise being the patron saint of Dubrovnik. This confirms my thesis that that is precisely what was targeted, the places where the flags were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, we will see that. Now, are you sure that's the UNESCO flag? If you're not sure, just say, "I'm not sure."

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: No. That is the flag that shows the places that are protected. I don't know whether it's called the UNESCO flag or something else, but I know that that is the flag that shows that that is a protected area, and it would be prohibited to devastate a place like that. I think it is called the UNESCO flag, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that's a legal question and we'll leave that to the lawyers. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC
utterances.text: See? See? This is the part that was destroyed here. That was destroyed. That is where the shell fell, a metre and a half or perhaps two metres below this flag that shows that this is a protected site. This is the very heart of the city. This is the real centre of the city, quite literally. This is where the big festival performances are held. This is where the great festival of Dubrovnik is open. On the left hand is the municipality, that is to say the main administrative building of Dubrovnik. Now, I am where the archives are. It's about 50 metres away.
